cues.text: By the second century, pagan writers were accusing Christians of a grim secret rite — eating human flesh and drinking human blood behind closed doors.
Early apologists like Tertullian and Minucius Felix had to answer the charge directly in their own writings.
The accusation is itself a kind of evidence.
Outsiders hostile to the new faith, listening to what Christians said about their central rite, understood “eat my flesh” and “drink my blood” literally enough to accuse them of cannibalism.
A community that believed it was merely eating a symbol is unlikely to have provoked that particular slander.
In the thirteenth century, St. Thomas Aquinas gave the Church's belief its classical philosophical expression, borrowing terms from Aristotle.
Every physical thing, in this framework, has accidents — its appearance, taste, weight, texture — and a substance underlying them, what the thing actually is.

Transubstantiation, in this account, is a change of substance without any change of accidents: the bread and wine's appearance, taste, and physical properties remain exactly what they were, while what they truly are changes completely.
It is not a claim that a microscope or a chemist would find anything unusual — it operates at a different level than physical measurement can reach.
What a Miracle Can and Cannot Prove
The Church has never treated events like those gathered in this exhibition as proof of the Real Presence the way a laboratory result proves a hypothesis.
It calls them motives of credibility — signs offered to a faith that already rests on Scripture, apostolic testimony, and the Church's own teaching authority.
A scientific study can describe what a relic is made of.
It cannot, by itself, establish why it is that way, and it cannot manufacture faith in someone unwilling to receive it as a sign.
That more modest claim is also its strength: the case for the Real Presence was never meant to depend on any single account, however striking.
